posts.hook: Launch/concept: the LLM only picks from a code-computed menu, math has the final word
posts.linkedin_post:
Launching VERITAS, my entry for the lablab.ai x Alpaca AI Trading Agents Hackathon (deadline Sep 4). It's an autonomous agent that trades 0-7 DTE vertical credit spreads on SPY and QQQ — on Alpaca paper trading, and I'll keep saying that every time.

The design decision I care most about: the LLM never touches a number. Each cycle, code computes a candidate menu of spreads with credit, width, max loss, breakeven, and edge — straight from the snapshot's bid/ask. Claude's entire action space is 'pick a menu item or abstain.' It can't invent strikes; custom legs are structurally rejected. Then a deterministic validator recomputes everything before any risk gate opens.

The LLM proposes. The math disposes.

Paper trading only — simulated fills don't model liquidity or fees, and none of this is financial advice. Repo and write-up in the comments.

posts.hook: Execution-aware twist: each documented simulator weakness maps to a specific guardrail
posts.linkedin_post:
Every broker simulator has documented gaps. Alpaca's own docs and issue tracker are unusually honest about theirs: paper fills ignore liquidity and NBBO size, multi-leg order replacement is hard-disabled, and option assignments don't arrive over the websocket.

Most hackathon agents treat those as noise. We treated them as spec.

So VERITAS — our lablab.ai x Alpaca entry — turns each documented weakness into a guardrail. Liquidity-blind fills became a 5-contract cap per leg plus a pre-trade slippage haircut: if the trade's edge dies under pessimistic fills, it never gets sent. The disabled mleg replace became a policy of never replacing an order — cancel, then a fresh one with a new idempotent client_order_id. Missing assignment events became REST activity polling every cycle, plus a 5-minute reconciliation loop where broker state is truth and internal state is just a hypothesis.

None of this makes the simulator more accurate. It makes the agent robust to the day it isn't a simulator. Still paper trading only, obviously — not financial advice.
posts.x_post: Most agents optimize for the simulator. VERITAS treats its documented gaps as spec: fills ignore liquidity, mleg replace is disabled, assignments skip the websocket. Each became a guardrail. @lablabai x @AlpacaHQ. Paper only. #BuildInPublic

posts.hook: Concrete internals: validator recompute, idempotent client_order_id, replayable JSONL audit trail
posts.linkedin_post:
Three implementation details doing more work than any prompt in VERITAS:

1. The validator. After Claude picks a spread, deterministic code recomputes credit, max loss, breakeven, and width from the raw leg quotes in the logged snapshot. If the LLM's numbers disagree with reality, the proposal dies — hallucinated economics cannot pass. The edge-ratio floor and the slippage haircut are checked against the recomputed values, not the proposed ones.

2. client_order_id. Every order carries a unique ID before it's sent, so a timeout followed by a retry can't create a duplicate fill. Orders are never replaced — Alpaca hard-disables mleg replacement — so the only recovery paths are cancel-then-fresh, then let the reconciliation loop sort out what actually happened.

3. The JSONL audit trail. Snapshot, features, LLM proposal, validator verdicts, risk verdicts, order, fill, exit, P&L — one JSON line per event, per cycle. Any trade can be replayed after the fact without trusting our summary of it.

That last one is the point of the whole project, honestly. An agent you can't audit is an agent you can't trust, and this is a hackathon build on paper trading — exactly the place to get the logging right. lablab.ai x Alpaca, submission Sep 4. Not financial advice.

posts.hook: Live GitHub Pages dashboard showing the full decision chain in real time
posts.linkedin_post:
New in VERITAS: a live dashboard, built as a static GitHub Pages site the agent's JSONL audit log renders into.

It shows the actual decision chain, not a summary of it — the market snapshot each cycle used, the computed features (trend, RSI, IV/RV), the candidate menu, Claude's thesis and confidence, the validator and risk-gate verdicts line by line, then orders, fills, exits, and P&L. If the agent abstains, you can see why: which gate said no.

I built it because 'trust me, the agent is running' is a weak claim for a hackathon submission. The audit log was already there for replay; pointing a static site at it was the cheapest way to make the whole loop inspectable while it runs.

Link in the comments. Paper trading only — the dashboard shows simulated fills, and none of this is financial advice. lablab.ai x Alpaca hackathon, deadline Sep 4.

posts.hook: Final stretch: agent runs autonomously through the deadline, the audit log is the submission
posts.linkedin_post:
Deadline day. Submissions for the lablab.ai x Alpaca hackathon close at 11:00 ET, and VERITAS doesn't know that — there's no calendar input in its feature set.

It will spend today the way it spent the last few: capture one snapshot per cycle, compute features, pick from the candidate menu or abstain, survive the validator and the risk gates, execute over the Alpaca MCP server, then reconcile against broker state every five minutes. Entry window 10:00-15:00 ET, 0DTE positions force-closed by 15:30, everything flat by 15:45. No keyboard. No overrides. The watchdog restarts it if the codespace dies.

The submission isn't a demo video of me clicking. It's the repo, the one-pager, and a JSONL file of every decision the agent made on its own — replayable line by line. That's the claim, and the log is the evidence.

Paper trading only, start to finish — simulated fills, no real money, not financial advice. Wrap-up post once the clock runs out.

video.recording_notes:
Recording setup (all free): OBS Studio, Display Capture for browser (dashboard, Alpaca docs, README) and Window Capture for VS Code/Codespace terminal. Record 1920x1080 at 30fps with a separate mic track and the noise-suppression filter on. Set browser zoom to 150 percent and terminal font to 16-18pt, dark theme throughout, so text survives compression. Record VO first, per scene, into separate tracks at the 140 wpm pacing (the per-scene scripts are pre-counted to fit), then cut video to VO — never trim the demo to save the VO.

Cut plan: assemble per-scene clips in DaVinci Resolve (free) or CapCut, cutting only at scene boundaries. Target assembly is 225s (~3:45), leaving ~15s of slack under the 4:00 cap. Add caption bullets over the three Alpaca weaknesses in scene 2 and the gate list in scene 5. Speed up long terminal scrolls 1.25-1.5x in scenes 3 and 7. Hold the end card 5 seconds.

Where things live: repo is github.com/akaheem/veritas-agent (cloned at the Codespace workspace root). Dashboard is already published at https://akaheem.github.io/veritas-agent/dashboard/index.html — record it in the browser, do not rebuild. The architecture diagram is the ASCII block in README.md — either screen-record the README view or rebuild it in Excalidraw for scene 5. The audit JSONL is written by the agent per cycle; locate it BEFORE recording (ls **/*.jsonl or git ls-files | grep jsonl) and note the absolute path for scenes 7 and 8. Alpaca limitation docs for scene 2 are on docs.alpaca.markets (paper trading: no market impact, liquidity-constrained fills, latency slippage; realtime vs historical bar caveats) plus any GitHub issues you want to show.

Pre-flight for the terminal scene: run uv run python -m veritas.main --help and confirm the exact --dry-run flag spelling as shipped (README documents --mode paper --once), then rehearse one full dry-run so you know how long it takes and where each stage prints. Record during US market hours, ideally 10:00-15:00 ET on a weekday, so option chains are live and the dashboard shows fresh rows; the README warns paper feeds can lag and realtime vs historical bars can disagree, so capture one clean cycle and keep the best take. A split tmux pane with tail -f on the audit JSONL during the dry-run makes the audit beat land visually.

Safety on camera: paper account only; blur or zoom past .env, API keys, and any account numbers if they appear in frame.

Placeholders to personalize before recording: scene 6 references 'this weekend' of cycles and a bounced trade — pick real rows from the live dashboard; scene 9's roadmap (a challenging model arguing against each proposal, walk-forward evaluation) is a suggested framing — swap in your actual roadmap. Free tooling recap: OBS Studio (record), DaVinci Resolve or CapCut (edit), Audacity (VO cleanup), Excalidraw (diagram), tmux (already in the Codespace).

slides.speaker_notes: This is the technology-implementation depth slide: VERITAS is a programmatic MCP client — not a CLI wrapper — holding one stdio session for the whole loop and submitting multi-leg limit orders with net credit as a negative limit price and per-leg position intent. cover.design_notes: Layout: (1) Wordmark "VERITAS" centered at ~y=535 in 236px bold monospace with wide letter-spacing, duplicated once — a blurred #6c8cff copy underneath for a soft glow and a crisp #eef2ff copy on top for thumbnail legibility; an accent rule with a diamond cap sits below it. (2) Subtitle "Execution-Aware Options Agent" in accent #6c8cff, tagline "LLM proposes · math disposes" in muted gray, both centered. (3) Decision pipeline: five rounded-rect nodes (SNAPSHOT → VALIDATE → SIZE → RISK → EXECUTE) with connector arrows, per-node captions, a dashed feedback loop from EXECUTE back to SNAPSHOT labeled "ack · feedback"; RISK is stroked in accent, EXECUTE in green to signal the terminal action. (4) P&L tick motif top-right: mini candlesticks plus "+$1,284.62" in #34d399 and "max DD" in #f4587a, balanced by a "$ veritas --mode=live" terminal prompt top-left. (5) Background: #0b0e14 with two-layer low-opacity accent grid, a faint descending candlestick band across the top, radial center glow, and a vignette; corner brackets and a bottom status strip (risk-armed dot, fills/latency readout) frame the composition. All text uses the JetBrains Mono/Consolas/monospace stack; no external assets, filters, or rasters — the one glow effect is a plain Gaussian blur that degrades gracefully. submission.long_description:
VERITAS is an autonomous AI trading agent that sells short-DTE (0–7 day) options credit spreads — bull puts and bear calls on SPY and QQQ — on Alpaca's paper-trading environment, running a complete loop (market analysis, opportunity detection, options selection, risk checks, execution, position management, P&L) with no human in the loop.

Its differentiator is that it is execution-aware. Instead of trusting simulator fills, VERITAS treats the documented weaknesses of broker paper trading — liquidity-blind fills, real-time vs historical bar inconsistency, un-replaceable multi-leg orders, and assignment events never streamed over websockets — plus the numerical-hallucination weakness of LLMs themselves, as risks to model and guard against. A pre-trade execution-reality simulator applies a conservative slippage haircut, and any trade whose edge dies under pessimistic fills is never sent. The LLM proposes; the math disposes.

The AI logic is deliberately constrained. Every ~15 minutes the agent captures one logged market snapshot as the single source of truth, computes deterministic features (EMA20/50 trend, RSI-14, implied vs realized volatility), and builds a menu of the best liquid credit spreads with credit, width, max loss, breakeven, and post-slippage edge computed entirely by code. Claude (claude-sonnet-5) may only pick a menu item or abstain (NO_TRADE is always available) and must write a falsifiable thesis; it cannot invent strikes or prices — a deterministic validator recomputes every number from raw leg quotes before anything proceeds, so hallucinated economics cannot pass.

Risk gates are hard limits enforced in code and not overridable by the LLM: $2,000 max loss per trade, a $2,000 daily-loss kill switch that flattens all positions, max 4 open spreads, portfolio heat ≤ 8% of equity, ≤ 5 contracts per leg, liquidity gates (OI ≥ 100, spread ≤ 30% of mid), a 10:00–15:00 ET entry window, and forced closes before expiry (0DTE flat by 15:30 ET). Exits trigger at 50% of credit (profit target) or 200% (stop).

Alpaca integration: execution runs through the Alpaca MCP Server (alpaca-mcp-server via the official MCP Python SDK) submitting multi-leg net-credit limit orders, with alpaca-py for market data. Orders carry idempotent client_order_ids, are never replaced (cancel + fresh), and a 5-minute reconciliation loop polls broker positions and activities so broker state is truth — catching assignments Alpaca does not stream. Every decision is written to a replayable JSONL audit log and surfaced on a live GitHub Pages dashboard. Paper trading only — MIT-licensed and fully open source.
